cheatsheet:
## Partial failure (lesson 1)

When a request gets no reply, six things look the same to the sender: the request was lost, the request is waiting in a queue, the other machine crashed, it's paused, the reply was lost, or the reply is slow. So every call to another machine has three outcomes: yes, no and unknown.

| Fact | What follows |
|---|---|
| TCP's ACK (acknowledgment) means the other machine's operating system got the bytes | It isn't an answer from the program |
| TCP removes duplicates only within one connection | A retry on a new connection is a new request |
| Networks hold packets in queues: in switches, in computers, in the software that runs virtual machines, and in TCP | Delay has no upper limit; no timeout tells slow from dead |
| A retry repeats whatever the request does | Send an idempotency key, one unique number per payment, with every attempt, and store it in the same transaction as the charge |

## Detecting failure (lesson 2)

- A timeout trades slow detection against false alarms. Pick it from measured delays, or let it adapt: TCP waits the smoothed round-trip time plus 4 times its variation, and phi accrual turns recent gaps between heartbeats ("I'm alive" messages) into a level of suspicion.
- SWIM asks k other members to check a silent machine before it accuses it, marks it suspect before dead, and lets it answer back with a higher incarnation number. Lifeguard makes an accuser that is struggling itself slow down.
- Gray failure: customers see errors while the detector sees a healthy machine. Judge health on the path real requests take.
- A paused machine looks exactly like a dead one. Detectors only suspect; correctness comes from majorities and fencing tokens.

## Clocks (lesson 3)

| Clock | In Java | Use it for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wall clock (time of day) | `System.currentTimeMillis()`, `Instant.now()` | points in time, times shown to people | jumps back and forward when it's corrected or a virtual machine moves |
| Monotonic clock | `System.nanoTime()` | durations and timeouts | means nothing across machines or reboots |

A computer's quartz clock drifts up to about 200 ppm (parts per million), about 17 s a day. NTP, the usual way to set a clock from time servers, keeps it within tens of ms over the internet. On AWS, it's under 100 µs over NTP and under 40 µs with the PTP hardware clock. Last write wins with each writer's own timestamps drops a write that came later whenever that writer's clock lags by more than the gap between the writes. Spanner commits only after waiting out its clock's error bound; CockroachDB assumes a maximum clock offset (500 ms by default) and shuts down nodes that drift past it. Give code a skewed clock in tests through `java.time.Clock`.

## Pauses, leases and fencing (lessons 4 and 5)

- A program can stop between any two instructions, for seconds, and can't tell: garbage collection, a shared cloud machine, a container's CPU quota, swapping memory to disk, `SIGSTOP`, waiting for the disk. ZGC's own pauses are under a millisecond on JDK 25; the other causes don't care which collector you run.
- A lease is a lock that runs out: `SET key token NX PX ttl` in Redis, a lease in etcd, a session in ZooKeeper. Release it with compare-and-delete (a Lua script, or `DELEX key IFEQ token` on Redis 8.4 and later), never a plain `DEL`.
- Check, then act, always leaves a gap. Renewing the lease and checking again shrink it; nothing inside the holder closes it.
- **Fencing token**: a number that grows with every new holder (Redis `INCR`, etcd's revision, ZooKeeper's zxid, an epoch) and travels with every write. The resource refuses any token lower than the highest it has seen. Only the resource can stop a late holder.

## Ordering without a shared clock (lesson 6)

| Stamp or id | Order it promises | What it can't tell you |
|---|---|---|
| Wall-clock timestamp | none across machines | cause before effect, once the clocks differ by more than a message takes |
| Lamport (counter, node) | causes before effects, in one total order | real time; whether two events were concurrent |
| Vector clock | causes before effects, and which events were concurrent | it costs one counter per node |
| Hybrid logical clock | Lamport's promise in 64 bits, close to wall-clock time | the real-time order of events no message connects |
| UUIDv7, Snowflake, ULID | time order within one generator at most | order across generators |
| One counter (a sequence, TiDB's timestamp oracle), or bounded clocks with a wait | real-time order | it costs a round trip to the counter, or the wait |

## System models (lesson 7)

| Timing model | What you may assume |
|---|---|
| Synchronous | known limits on message delay, pauses and clock error (no real system has them) |
| Partially synchronous | the limits usually hold, but can be broken for a while (the realistic one) |
| Asynchronous | no limits, no clocks, no timeouts |

| Node model | A faulty node |
|---|---|
| Crash-stop | stops and never comes back |
| Crash-recovery | restarts; keeps what it put on disk with `fsync`, loses its memory (the realistic one) |
| Byzantine | does anything, including lie |

- Safety: nothing bad ever happens; it must hold in every run. Liveness: something good eventually happens; it may wait for timing to behave. "Eventually" means liveness.
- FLP: with no limits on time and one possible crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that agreement finishes. Raft and Paxos stay safe always, and use timeouts only to make progress.
- Put anything another node may count (a vote, a "saved") on disk before you send it.
- Surviving f crashed nodes takes 2f + 1 nodes; surviving f lying nodes takes 3f + 1 (PBFT, with replies from 2f + 1). Most databases skip the second, and use checksums (CRC-32C, carried end to end), checks on meaning and access control against small lies.

## Testing (lesson 8)

| Method | Checks | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| Model checking (TLA+, P) | the design, in every schedule of a small model | bugs in the code; bugs that need a bigger model |
| Deterministic simulation (FoundationDB, TigerBeetle's VOPR, Antithesis) | the real code, in millions of seeded runs that replay exactly | faults and work nobody put in the simulator |
| Jepsen and Elle | the real system under real faults, judged from the client history | damage no client saw; it can't prove there are no bugs |
| Property tests (jqwik, Kotest) | one part of the program on made-up inputs, shrunk to the smallest failure | problems between parts |
| Fault injection (Toxiproxy), chaos experiments | your code, and the people running it, under one real fault | rare combinations of faults |

A simulator is deterministic only if every random choice and every clock read goes through the seed: run one seed twice and compare the whole trace.
recap: A system on several computers fails in part, and each computer knows only the messages that have reached it. Silence has six causes, so every call to another machine can end in unknown. An idempotency key, one per payment and sent with every attempt, makes a retry safe.

A failure detector turns silence into suspicion. Pick timeouts from measured delays or let them adapt (phi accrual, SWIM with Lifeguard), and expect them to be wrong: correctness must come from majorities and fencing.

The wall clock gives points in time and jumps; the monotonic clock gives durations. Anything that orders writes by timestamp is only as good as its clock's error bound: last write wins loses writes, and Spanner waits out the bound.
A program can stop for seconds at any instruction without knowing it: garbage collection, a shared cloud machine and a stuck disk can all do it. So a lock holder can act after its lease ran out.
Leases need fencing tokens: the resource refuses any token lower than the highest it has seen. Only the thing being written can stop a late holder.

Lamport and hybrid logical clocks put causes before effects, vector clocks spot concurrent events, and only one counter or a bounded clock with a wait gives real-time order. Time-ordered ids order one generator at most.

Algorithms are proved against a system model, and the realistic one is partial synchrony with crash-recovery nodes. Safety must always hold, liveness may wait for timing to behave (FLP), and lying nodes take 3f + 1 to out-vote.

Test in layers: model checking for the design, deterministic simulation for the code, Jepsen-style testing for the real system, plus property tests, fault injection and chaos experiments. Each finds only the faults it was given.

quiz.q: A payments program asks the card's bank to approve a payment, and gets no reply within 2 seconds. What does it know about the payment?
options: The bank is down, so the payment failed
The card was not charged, so sending the same request again is safe
Nothing for certain: the request or the reply may be lost or late, or the bank's computer may be paused or crashed, so the charge may or may not have happened
The network dropped the request
quiz.why: Silence fits six situations, and in two of them (reply lost, reply slow) the bank charged the card. The program can't tell which from its side, so the outcome is unknown. That's why a retry must carry the same idempotency key, a unique number for the payment, so the bank can recognise it. Deciding the payment failed, the most tempting option, is how cards get charged twice.

quiz.q: The program retries a timed-out payment over a new TCP connection. TCP is the set of rules that delivers a stream of bytes complete and in order. Why doesn't it stop the bank from charging twice?
options: TCP removes duplicates only within one connection; the retry is a new request on a new connection
TCP never removes duplicate pieces of data
TCP would stop it, but only if Nagle's algorithm, a setting that holds back small writes, is off
TLS, the encryption on top, turns off TCP's duplicate detection
quiz.why: TCP's numbering removes duplicate pieces inside one connection, and its acknowledgment means only that the other computer's operating system received the bytes. A retry after a timeout usually opens a new connection, and to the bank's program it's a brand-new request. Only an idempotency key, stored with the charge, makes the retry safe.

quiz.q: A group of computers declares one dead after 3 seconds without a heartbeat, its regular "I'm alive" message. The Java programs on them sometimes pause for 5 seconds. What follows?
options: Nothing, because heartbeats are sent from a separate thread
The detector will sometimes declare a live, paused computer dead, so correctness can't depend on the detector being right
The paused computer will notice the pause and stop itself in time
Phi accrual would never make this mistake
quiz.why: A paused program sends nothing, so from outside it looks exactly like a crashed one. Any detector faster than the longest pause will sometimes suspect a computer that is alive. An adaptive detector such as phi accrual only makes the trade smarter, not free. The heartbeat thread, a separate path of work in the same program, stops with the rest of it, and a program learns of its pause only after it runs again. So the system must stay correct when the detector is wrong: majorities and fencing.

quiz.q: Every health check for the program that approves payments says it's fine, yet about 5% of payments fail, all through one faulty network path. What should change?
options: Lower the health-check timeout
Add more copies of the program
Send health checks more often
Judge health from the real request path, with real or made-up payments, instead of a separate check
quiz.why: This is gray failure: the detector and the customers see different things, because the health check doesn't travel the broken path. Checking more often or with a shorter timeout repeats the same blind check, and more copies behind the same path don't help. Health measured on the path real payments take sees the failure.

quiz.q: Which Java call should measure how long the call to the bank took?
options: `System.nanoTime()`
`System.currentTimeMillis()`
`Instant.now()`
`LocalDateTime.now()`
quiz.why: `nanoTime` reads the monotonic clock, which never jumps, so the difference of two readings is a true duration. The other three read the wall clock, which NTP or a moved virtual machine can step forward or back in the middle of the call. That gives a duration that is too long, too short or even negative. The wall clock is for points in time, not intervals.

quiz.q: Two programs update one record in a store that keeps the write with the highest timestamp from the writer's own clock (last write wins). Program B's clock runs 5 s behind. B reads A's value and writes a new one 1 s later. What happens?
options: B's write wins, because it happened later
Both writes are kept side by side for the programs to merge
B's write carries the older timestamp and is silently dropped, although B was told it succeeded
The store rejects B's write with a clock error
quiz.why: Last write wins compares timestamps, not causes. B's clock says its write happened about 4 seconds before A's, so the store keeps A's value and throws B's away after confirming it. Keeping both side by side needs version vectors, and few stores check clocks on writes. Jepsen's 2013 test of Cassandra, a database that uses last write wins, lost about 28% of confirmed writes this way.

quiz.q: A worker checks that its lease, a lock that runs out, is still valid. Then its virtual machine stalls for 15 seconds before it writes, and meanwhile another worker takes the lease and writes. What stops the first worker's late write?
options: A lease of 60 seconds instead of 10
The storage refusing the write, because its fencing token is lower than one it has already seen
Checking the lease once more right before the write
Running Java with the ZGC garbage collector
quiz.why: The pause landed after the last check, so nothing inside the worker can catch it, and no lease length is safe against a pause with no limit. A second check narrows the gap, but a pause can still fall after it, and ZGC doesn't help with a stalled virtual machine. The storage is the only party that sees both writes, so it must compare tokens: the new holder's token is higher, and the late one is refused.

quiz.q: Events a and b happened on different computers, and no chain of messages connects them. What do their Lamport timestamps, counters that jump past every message they hear of, tell you?
options: Which of them happened first in real time
That they were concurrent
That a happened first, if L(a) < L(b)
Nothing about their real order: either can have the smaller stamp, and only vector clocks show they were concurrent
quiz.why: Lamport stamps promise one direction only: if a happened before b, then L(a) < L(b). For unconnected events the order of the stamps is an accident of counting, so L(a) < L(b) doesn't mean a came first, and the stamps can't reveal concurrency at all. Vector clocks can, at the cost of one counter per computer. Real-time order across unconnected events needs one counter, or a bounded clock with a wait.

quiz.q: A computer taking part in an election records its vote in memory, replies, and writes the vote to disk a few milliseconds later. Under which fault model is that safe?
options: Crash-stop only
Crash-recovery
Every model, because the gap is only milliseconds
Byzantine, since votes are signed
quiz.why: Under crash-stop, a computer that crashes in the gap never comes back, so its vote can't be cast twice. Under crash-recovery, a crash between the reply and the write makes it restart without the vote and vote again, which can elect two leaders in one term. A short gap only makes the bug rare, not impossible. Raft requires the vote to be on disk before the reply.

quiz.q: A program that stores messages on several computers says "saved" at once, but by default calls `fsync`, which puts the data on disk, only every two minutes. Which testing method is most likely to show that it loses messages it reported saved?
options: A property-based test of the code that turns its messages into bytes
Jepsen-style testing with a nemesis that fakes power cuts by dropping writes not yet on disk
A TLA+ model of how it copies messages
Small tests of each computer's request-handling code
quiz.why: The bug lives in the default settings of the running system, not in the design or one part. The copying rules may be correct, but the two-minute `fsync` breaks their assumption that saved data is on disk. A black-box test that kills machines and drops unsaved writes, as Jepsen did to NATS with LazyFS, shows it. A TLA+ model would assume writes reach the disk, and the byte encoding and request handling are fine on their own.
